Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Violence: Violence
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Jamal Adebayo, a twenty-year-old physician, felt the cold weight of the past settle heavily upon him even now, months after returning from his deployment as a medic. He had been so young, barely out of medical school, when he found himself in the midst of a chaotic ambush. He was crouched low, the ground vibrating with explosions, desperately trying to save Private Miller. Miller’s face was etched in Jamal’s mind, his eyes wide, his chest heaving, struggling for every ragged breath as the dust and smoke filled the air around them. The violence was absolute, relentless, a cacophony of gunfire and screams. Then, a sudden, concussive blast nearby, and for a few agonizing seconds, a complete, eerie silence descended, broken only by Miller’s failing gasps. Jamal had tried everything, but Miller slipped away. He could recall fragments: the terror in Miller’s eyes, the metallic taste of fear in his own mouth, the suffocating feeling of helplessness. But the full picture remained elusive; he found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, and his memories of the event came in disconnected pieces that did not fit together. There were parts of the event that he simply could not remember no matter how hard he tried, leaving gaping holes in his understanding of what happened.

Returning home, Jamal found the world profoundly altered. He had always believed in order, in the ability of medicine to heal, but the brutal reality of combat had completely destroyed his beliefs about how the world works. He looked in the mirror and often felt a stranger staring back; he truly felt like he didn't know himself anymore. The eager, optimistic medical student was gone, replaced by a constant, gnawing sense of dread. He had come to believe that he had to be on guard all the time, scanning his surroundings, anticipating danger even in the most benign settings.

This hypervigilance made his work as a doctor particularly challenging. A quiet moment in the hospital corridor, or the sudden hush in a patient’s room after a visitor left, would trigger a primal fear. The complete silence would transport him back to those terrifying seconds after the blast, his heart hammering against his ribs, convinced that disaster was imminent. He found himself avoiding the quieter wards, preferring the bustling energy of the emergency department, though even there, certain situations were fraught. When a patient presented with difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, the sight and sound of their struggle would instantly flood him with the visceral memory of Private Miller, leaving him momentarily paralyzed, his own breath catching in his throat. Even indirect violence, like an angry family member raising their voice or the aggressive tone of a fellow doctor, could send a jolt of adrenaline through him, making him tense and irritable.

Over weeks and months, Jamal began to adapt in subtle ways to manage these intense reactions. He’d learned to delegate patients with respiratory distress whenever possible, finding excuses to pass them off to colleagues, though the guilt gnawed at him. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator if it meant avoiding the potential for a sudden, enclosed silence. His colleagues noticed his increasing withdrawal; he’d stopped joining them for lunch, preferring to eat quickly in the noisy hospital cafeteria rather than risk a quiet moment with a single co-worker. He found himself mentally replaying conversations, searching for hidden threats, and this constant vigilance began to take a toll on his focus, leading to small but noticeable errors in charting and patient communication. He felt isolated, adrift, and increasingly exhausted by the relentless internal battle.

It was a particularly quiet night shift, the hospital unusually still, when Jamal found himself alone in an empty consultation room. The sudden silence was deafening, overwhelming, and for a terrifying moment, he was back in that dusty, violent landscape. He doubled over, gasping for air, convinced he was suffocating. The sheer terror and the realization of how profoundly his life had been consumed by these unseen forces finally drove him to seek help. What frightened him most was the fear that he was losing his ability to be the doctor he desperately wanted to be, the doctor he used to be.
